chunks: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Imran al-Daqqaq, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Abd Allah al-Kufi said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Barmaki said: al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan said: Bakr, on the authority of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Barqi, on the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn Bahr, on the authority of Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)
I said: His Word, the Mighty and High: 'O Iblis! What prevented you that you should do obeisance to him whom I created with My Two Hands?'

He (AS) replied: The hand in the speech of the Arabs means power and bounty. He said: 'And remember Our servant Dawud, the Possessor of Power.' And He said: 'And the Heaven, We raised it high with power,' meaning with power. And He said: 'And whom He has strengthened with an inspiration from Him,' meaning He strengthened them. And it is said: So-and-so has many hands with me, meaning excess and beneficence, and so-and-so has a white hand with me, meaning bounty.
ai.seo_question: What does 'created with My Two Hands' mean in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) elucidates that the 'Two Hands' (Yadayn) in the verse regarding Iblis and Adam are metaphorical, signifying divine power and bounty rather than physical limbs. He supports this by citing Quranic verses where 'hand' (yad/ayd) is used to denote strength or favor, and by referencing Arabic idioms where 'hand' implies generosity or abundance. This interpretation aligns with the Shia theological principle of tanzih (divine transcendence), rejecting anthropomorphism by grounding the term in linguistic usage found in the Quran and classical Arabic. The narration further highlights the semantic flexibility of 'yad' in Arabic, ranging from physical strength to spiritual favor, reinforcing the non-literal understanding of divine attributes.
